raw_response.rationale: The full 50-page NBER working paper text (June 2008) is readable in prose (though the appended formatted table/figure pages at PDF pp. 39-46, 48, and 50 are blank in the PDF text layer, every specification and variable is fully detailed in Sections 2-5 and Appendix A). Although the paper conducts multiple inferential econometric analyses (OLS, spatial MLE, 2SLS, LIML), none tests a narrow Criterion 2 rule-type legal/tenure/tariff/ownership/regulatory exposure on a Criterion 4 water/sanitation service access outcome: (1) Section 4 (Tables 4a-6) models the 1991 share of small (1-3 room) houses with a central water connection (Criterion 4), but the explanatory variables are neighboring localities' water coverage rates (W'b reaction-function slope), log median household income, log number of urban households, their wealth-by-size interaction, population density, and 1982 anti-military legislative vote share—socioeconomic, demographic, partisan-voting, and spatial-lag predictors rather than a rule-type legal, tenure, zoning, tariff, or ownership variable (pre-1988 national illegality of servicing informal settlements is nationwide background context and not a regression variable); (2) Section 5 (Tables 7-8) reverses the exposure-outcome relationship by using 1991 water servicing of small (or untitled) houses as the predictor of 1991-2000 locality urban household growth (failing Criterion 4); (3) Appendix A (Table A1) estimates hedonic log-rent regressions measuring consumer willingness-to-pay for water/sewer connections (explicitly failing Criterion 4); (4) Appendix B (Table B2) first-stage regressions predict water servicing from porous geology, solar insolation, distance to Sao Paulo, and 1970 census demographics (failing Criterion 2); and (5) Tables 1-3 are purely descriptive cross-tabulations (Table 3 examines municipal minimum lot-size laws >125 m2 only against descriptive migrant and untitled-homeowner ratios, with no water/sanitation outcome).
